title: Start with the idea behind this app
summary: Look from big to small: market → industry → fundamentals → structure. The app tells you what happened and why; the decision is yours
body:
**In one line**

The most common mistake in investing is staring at one stock's moves and ignoring the environment around it. This app splits looking at the market into four steps, from big to small:

• **Market**: is the overall wind behind you or against you?
• **Industry**: which industries is money flowing into?
• **Fundamentals**: is the company itself any good?
• **Structure**: where on its path is the price right now?

Every step has a 'How it's calculated' link showing where the numbers come from. For words you do not know, tap the question mark next to them or look them up in the Glossary.

**What this app does not do**

It does not tell you which stock to buy or when to trade, and it does not predict prices. It organizes public data and explains the rules so that you can understand and then judge for yourself. The same information should lead different people with different finances to different decisions.

**How to read this primer**

Read in order; it takes about ten minutes. Afterwards you will know what every color, number and label on the radar means, and also what each of them can **not** tell you.

title: What is in this app
summary: What each of the five tabs does and where to start
body:
**In one line**

This app turns price action in US, China A-share and Hong Kong stocks into something you can read: how the environment is, which industries are strong, which companies are good, and where the price is on its path. It only lays out facts and knowledge; it does not recommend trades.

**The five tabs**

• **Analysis** (the app opens here): enter a stock symbol to see its Chan analysis: chart, conclusion, buy/sell points, fundamentals and analyst ratings. Start here when you want to study one specific stock.
• **Radar**: see at a glance which stocks in a market recently showed structure signals. At the top are the market environment and an industry strip; in the middle is a bubble chart where each bubble is one signal of one stock. Start here when you want the big picture first, then individual stocks.
• **Watchlist**: stocks you starred with ☆ on the analysis page. They are grouped into 'Signals in the last 5 days' and 'No new signals' (by market while signals are still loading), with market-environment hints on top so you can check back regularly.
• **Learn**: where you are now: the beginner primer, the glossary and the Chan primer. Come back here for any word or chart you do not understand.
• **Me**: your account info, then the **Language** switch, **Signal rules** (Strict / Balanced / Relaxed: what counts as a buy or sell point) and **Help** (contact us) right on the page, followed by four sub-pages: **Subscription** (current plan, restore purchases), **Preferences** (the 'Show pro details' switch, which shows numbers such as area ratio and price ratio), **About** (version, privacy policy, terms, disclaimer) and **Account & Security** (delete account).

![Analyze: enter a symbol, pick daily or weekly](guide-tab-analysis)

![Radar: market, industries, bubble chart, date rail](guide-tab-radar)

![Watchlist: market environment on top](guide-tab-watchlist)

![Me: language, signal rules, help and four sub-pages](guide-tab-profile)

**Two common ways to use it**

• Big picture first: Radar (market → industry → stocks with strong fundamentals) → tap a bubble to open the stock's detail page → compare the conclusion with the chart.
• Stock first: enter a symbol on Analysis → read the detail page → go back to the radar to see its industry and the market environment.

**Every number can be traced**

Calculated conclusions in the app (states, grades, strength, buy/sell point types…) almost always have a 'How it's calculated' link showing the derivation steps and limitations. Tap the question mark next to words you do not know.

**What this app does not do**

It does not tell you which stock to buy or when to trade, and it does not predict prices. Everything is for learning only and is not investment advice.

title: How to read the radar page
summary: What the market card, industry strip, date rail, bubbles and list are
body:
**The radar answers four questions**: how is the market? how are the industries? which companies have strong fundamentals? have they shown structure signals recently? The page answers them from top to bottom.

![Top to bottom: market card → industry strip → bubble chart → date rail](guide-tab-radar)

**Market card at the top**: choose a market (US / A-share / Hong Kong / Watchlist); it shows the current risk-on / neutral / risk-off state and its probability. Open it for the sentiment score, five drivers (rates, spread, dollar, volatility, oil) and the macro calendar for the next 7 days. The current index name sits under the market name; tap it to switch index (e.g. S&P 500, Nasdaq 100).

![The market environment panel opened from the market card](guide-radar-market)

**Industry strip**: 'All industries' plus a pill per industry, ranked from strongest to weakest versus the market over the last 20 trading days. Tap one and the radar and list show only that industry; the industry button at the end opens the full industry-strength board.

![Industry board: ranked by 20-day strength versus the market](guide-radar-sectors)

**Date rail**: choose which day's signals to view. A signal stays valid for 5 trading days, so one stock's signal shows on several consecutive days. For free users the sample day is always the first cell.

**Bubble chart**: each bubble is one signal of one stock.
• Red is buy-type, green is sell-type; **shade is signal strength**.
• **Size is the type**: type 1 smallest, type 3 largest; later means more confirmed.
• **Position**: the closer to the center, the newer the signal.
• The small capsule '▲n / ▼n' at the top right is the net number of analyst upgrades / downgrades in 90 days (US only); 'Aligned' means the daily direction agrees with the 30-minute chart; 'New' means it appeared today.
• The letter on the last line of a bubble is the stock's current composite fundamentals grade.
• Tapping a bubble opens that stock's analysis page.

**Why only some stocks appear**: the radar only shows buy/sell points of stocks with strong fundamentals (the threshold adapts to the pool: usually the top 25%, at least 8, never below B). This narrows what you look at; it is not a recommendation.

**List**: the button at the bottom left of the canvas lists the stocks that pass the fundamentals threshold in three groups: 'recent buy point', 'only sell points recently', 'none'; with an industry selected it lists only that industry. Members can open it any time; free users can open it on the sample day, with buy/sell points as of that day.

**Pending**: signals that have not finished are not drawn on the radar; only their count is shown above.

**Tap the title 'Chan radar ▾'**: the menu switches between the Chan radar, the Fundamentals radar and the Rating radar. The first time you open the radar page, a flow chart of the reading order (market → industry → fundamentals → structure) opens once to show how to read the page; tap outside to close.

![The reading order shown the first time you open the radar](guide-radar-flow)

**Common questions**
• A radar signal may not match the detail page: a bubble is a snapshot from the latest scan, while the detail page recalculates with the newest candles, and structure on the latest few candles can be rewritten.
• The radar is empty: there may simply be no qualifying signals in these days, or a scan may be running; look again later.

**What this page does not do**: no ranking and no recommendations; it only lays out facts by time.

**Fundamentals Radar**: tap the page title and pick "Fundamentals Radar" to see which companies' fundamentals changed recently: our overall grade rose (red) or fell (green) versus a while ago, shown together and told apart by color. The three rings are the last week / month / 3 months; **bubble size is the overall grade and a darker color means a bigger change**. After a rating-method change it takes a few days to rebuild history, so this may be empty right after an adjustment.

**Rating Radar**: pick "Rating Radar" to see changes in broker (analyst) ratings: Red bubbles are stocks recently net-upgraded by brokers and green ones net-downgraded (a stock with both gets two bubbles). Same three rings; a darker color means more brokers net-changed, and "View list and changes" shows which brokers. Only US stocks have this data for now; A-shares / HK stocks show a notice.

Both radars share the index under the market bar and only look at its constituents. "Featured" at the top right draws only companies whose overall grade reaches the threshold (the same threshold as the fundamentals list); tap it to see all. Tapping a sector chip filters too. Tap a bubble to open that stock's fundamental research (Fundamentals Radar) or analyst ratings (Rating Radar); "How it works" explains the thresholds. After the rating method is adjusted it takes a few days to rebuild history, so "Grade changes" may be empty right after an adjustment. They only lay out facts about change and do not mean the price will rise or fall.

**Signal rules**

Under Me → Signal rules you can choose Strict / Balanced / Relaxed. This decides what counts as a buy or sell point: Strict gives the fewest and is closest to the textbook; Balanced (default) gives about twice as many; Relaxed gives the most and the earliest, but is easier to overturn. Each option is explained on that settings page; the radar and the stock detail pages follow your choice.

title: How to read a stock's analysis page
summary: Chart, conclusion card, buy/sell points, fundamentals and analyst ratings, step by step in page order
body:
**From top to bottom**

**1. Conclusion card**: the card at the top says in one sentence where the price is on its path, e.g. 'Price left the pivot upward; waiting for a pullback to confirm'. It describes structure; it is not telling you to buy or sell. The left cell, 'Latest signal', shows the most recent buy/sell point (one that has not finished is 'pending' and does not count); the right cell, '30-min check', is the sub-level confirmation in item 7.

![Conclusion card and chart: the vertical dashed line is the day picked on the radar](guide-detail-top)

**2. Chart**: candles plus the structure Chan theory draws.
• **Strokes**: the ups and downs joined into line segments.
• **Pivot**: the range where several strokes keep swinging, drawn as a box.
• **Buy/sell points**: red badges are buy-type, green badges are sell-type, labelled like 'type-1 buy' or 'type-2 sell'.
• **Dashed = not confirmed yet**: gray dashed badges are 'pending' and carry no red or green.
• Layer switches sit above the chart: strokes, pivots, signals; 'More layers' adds fractals, segments and divergence. Divergence draws the b and c legs and labels the area ratio.
• Below the chart is the indicator bar: MA, EMA and BOLL — tap to switch each on or off; all are off by default.
• **Compare**: the dropdown at the far right of the row above the chart, for setting other ways of reading the market against Chan; for now Wyckoff and SMC, with more possible later. Pick one and the Chan layers are tucked away so only it is drawn; pick "Chan (default)" to bring them back. Only one can be on at a time so one chart does not stack several structures, and the app returns to Chan after a restart. They only mark positions and are not buy or sell signals.
  ◦ **Wyckoff**: shades the detected trading range and marks the events inside it (SC, Spring, SOS…); tap a mark for a plain-language explanation. It shows which stage the structure looks like it is in, lags, and can be wrong.
  ◦ **SMC**: marks breaks / changes of structure (BOS / CHoCH), order blocks, price gaps (FVG) and similar positions from the candles' own highs and lows; once SMC is picked, the dropdown gains an "SMC display" item to also show equal highs / lows, liquidity sweeps, premium / discount zones, strong / weak highs and lows and previous-period highs / lows. Wyckoff shades the detected trading range and marks the events inside it (SC, Spring, SOS…); tap a mark for a plain-language explanation. It shows which stage the structure looks like it is in, lags, and can be wrong — it is not a buy or sell signal.
• **SMC**: marks breaks / changes of structure (BOS / CHoCH), order blocks, price gaps (FVG) and similar positions from the candles' own highs and lows; the settings button on the right lets you also show equal highs / lows, liquidity sweeps, premium / discount zones, strong / weak highs and lows and previous-period highs / lows. Turning on Wyckoff or SMC tucks the Chan layers away first (tap again to bring them back), and the two are never on together, so one chart does not stack several structures. They only mark positions and are not buy or sell signals.
• Tap a chart element for its explanation; the chart can go full screen.
• Pick the time frame on the Analyze tab when you enter a symbol: daily or weekly (30 minutes is only used for the sub-level check).

![The 'More layers' menu](guide-detail-layers)

**3. Three views (switch at the top)**
• **Chan structure**: everything below is about price structure.
• **Fundamentals research**: valuation, growth, profitability, momentum, estimate revisions and financial health, ranked within the industry on six dimensions and combined, weighted by the company's stage, into a grade from A+ to F, with drill-downs.
• **Analyst ratings**: broker rating distribution, recent rating changes and price targets.

![Fundamentals: composite grade and six-factor chart](guide-quant-overview)

![Analyst ratings: distribution, price targets, earnings vs estimates](guide-analyst)

**4. 'What this means'**: translates the current stage into plain language and says what it does not imply.

!['What this means'](guide-detail-meaning)

**5. Buy/sell point list**: shows the latest few by default; each has type, established date, price and strength. Open one to see how it was identified (with that signal's own numbers). Note the two dates: the **established date** is the day the signal was confirmed, the **extreme date** is the candle where the badge sits, usually a few candles left of the established date.

![One signal opened: how it was identified, its established date and chart date](guide-detail-signal)

**6. Stage flow chart**: collapsed by default. Expanded, it shows where the price is on 'pivot forms → swings → leaves → pullback or rebound confirms'.

![Stage flow chart: the current step is highlighted](guide-detail-flow)

**7. Sub-level confirmation (members)**: in the '30-min check' cell of the conclusion card. the daily direction compared with recent buy/sell points on the 30-minute chart (weekly compared with daily). Same direction is 'aligned', opposite is 'against the trend', none yet is 'waiting'. It only says whether two levels point the same way; it guarantees nothing.

**8. Worth noting**: pending items and risks for this stock.

**Buttons at top right**
• ☆ adds to the watchlist; tap again to remove.
• Share: makes an analysis image with a QR code.

**Free and members**

Free users can analyze a few new stocks per day (the quota is shown above the analysis page); stocks already analyzed today stay viewable. Subscribers get unlimited analyses and unlock sub-level confirmation and the fundamentals list on the radar.

**After reading**

Every term and chart element can be looked up in the Glossary and the Chan primer. To understand how structure relates to the market, industry and fundamentals, read 'How the four layers relate'.

title: Market conditions: tailwind or headwind
summary: What risk-on, neutral and risk-off mean, and how to read the probability
body:
**Why start with the market**

Most stocks move with the market. When the market is poor even a good company can fall; when it is strong, ordinary companies tend to rise too. Looking at conditions first tells you whether you have a tailwind or a headwind.

**Risk-on / neutral / risk-off**

• **Risk-on**: money is willing to chase returns and favors offensive sectors such as tech and discretionary.
• **Risk-off**: money prefers steadier places: utilities, staples and cash.
• **Neutral**: no clear lean; everyone is waiting for a direction.

![Market panel: state, probabilities, past year and sentiment](guide-radar-market)

How is it decided? Over the last 20 trading days it looks at whether offensive or defensive sectors gained more, whether money is fleeing to short-term bonds, plus the market's return and volatility. A statistical model sums this up into three states and gives each a probability.

**Reading the probability**

'Risk-on 90%' means today's data is 90% similar to the historical situations labelled risk-on. It does **not** mean a 90% chance of rising.

**Why sentiment and market state sometimes disagree**

Sentiment (the fear & greed index) measures mood; market state measures where money is going. Early in a recovery after a fall, money has started returning to offensive sectors but people have not calmed down yet, so you can see risk-on with fear. That is not a data error; they are two different things.

**Drivers**

Interest rates, the dollar, volatility and oil are external conditions that affect overall valuations. Open any of them to see today's value, the value 20 days ago, how up or down is decided and what it usually means for stocks.

![Drivers and the 7-day macro calendar](guide-radar-drivers)

**Common mistakes**

• Treating 'risk-on' as a buy signal: it only describes recent money preferences.
• Seeing 'risk-off' and expecting an immediate crash: it only says money is cautious.

title: Industry: where is money flowing
summary: How to read relative strength and why compare industries
body:
**Why look at industries**

Within one market, industries often differ a lot: some rise for months, others keep lagging. Knowing which industries money favors helps you see how much of a stock's move comes from its industry.

**Relative strength = industry return − market return**

Over the last 20 trading days. If tech rose 5% and the market rose 3%, tech's relative strength is +2%, so it beat the market; a negative number means it lagged. The industry list is ranked by this number from strongest to weakest.

![Industry board: industry, state, signal count and relative strength per row](guide-radar-sectors)

**Industry state**

Each industry also has its own risk-on / neutral / risk-off, computed separately with the same kind of model as the market, using the industry's return, volatility, fear gauge, relative strength and money flow.

**How industries are grouped**

US stocks use 11 level-1 industries (GICS), A-shares use Shenwan level 1 and Hong Kong uses Hang Seng level 1. The same company can have different industry names under different standards.

**What happens when you tap an industry**

On the radar, tapping an industry limits the radar and the list to that industry's stocks so you can compare peers side by side.

**Common mistakes**

• Leading industries keep leading: leadership rotates, and recent strength does not mean it continues.
• A weak industry means never look: a weak industry does not mean every company in it is weak, only that the backdrop is not helping.

title: Fundamentals: is the company itself any good
summary: The six dimensions, the composite grade, and why good fundamentals do not mean a rising price
body:
**What fundamentals are**

Fundamentals are about the company itself: does its business make money, is it growing, is the price expensive. They are separate from recent price moves.

**Six dimensions**

• **Valuation**: is the price expensive relative to what the company earns (often the P/E).
• **Growth**: how fast sales and profit grow.
• **Profitability**: how efficiently it makes money, e.g. profit left from every 100 of sales.
• **Momentum**: the tendency of price moves over recent months.
• **Earnings-estimate revisions**: whether analysts raise or lower forecasts of future profit.
• **Financial health**: how much it owes, how heavy the interest is, how long its cash lasts, and whether profit turns into real cash (not applicable to banks and insurers).

None of these looks at an absolute number; each looks at where the company ranks **within its industry** (percentile): 85 means stronger than 85% of companies in the industry.

![Six-factor report card: each line gives the stock's number and its place in the sector](guide-quant-scores)

**Composite grade**

The six are averaged with weights set by the company's stage: fast-growing companies lean on growth, mature ones on valuation and profitability, and ones short of cash or heavy with debt on financial health; tap the composite grade to see each share. The result maps to 13 letters from A+ to F; A+ is roughly the top 7% of the industry. If an item with a meaningful weight is as low as F, the composite is capped at C+ so one very weak item cannot hide behind the others.

Tap a stage under 'Company stage' to see the top 30 companies in that stage by composite score and where this stock ranks, so you can see roughly where it sits among similar companies; tap a company in the list to open its analysis (counts toward the daily free quota for free users). It only reflects this model's composite score; it is not a recommendation list.

![Composite grade and six-factor chart (dashed line = sector median)](guide-quant-overview)

**The Fundamentals threshold on the radar**

The radar only draws structure signals of stocks with strong fundamentals: the top 25% of rated stocks, at least 8, never below B. This narrows the scope; it is not a recommendation list. Tap 'Fundamentals' in the flow chart to see the current threshold and count.

**Why good fundamentals do not mean the price will rise**

• A good company can already be expensive, with good news in the price.
• Short-term prices are often driven by sentiment and money flow, not company quality.
• The grade is a snapshot; companies change.

So fundamentals work more like a **filter**: they help you avoid companies with obvious problems, not give a reason to buy.

title: Structure signals: where is the price on its path
summary: What Chan buy/sell points are and are not, and how to read confirmation and alignment
body:
**What it is**

Chan theory is a way to describe the shape of a price path: ups and downs are split into 'strokes', a range where price keeps swinging is a 'pivot', and then it looks at how the force changes after price leaves the pivot. Marks such as 'type-1 buy' or 'type-2 sell' on the radar are **positions** identified on the path by these rules.

![Strokes, pivots and signals on the analysis page](guide-detail-top)

**What it is not**

It is not an order to buy or sell and it does not predict prices. A 'type-1 buy' only says: in a downtrend, this leg has less force than the previous one. Whether a rebound or more decline follows, it does not know.

**The three types in one line each**

• **Type 1**: in a trend, the last leg has less force than the one before (trend divergence).
• **Type 2**: the first pullback (or rebound) after type 1 that does not break the type-1 extreme.
• **Type 3**: the first pullback (or rebound) after price leaves a pivot that does not return into it.

Later types are more confirmed but also closer to the later part of a move.

**Established vs pending**

A point counts only after its stroke finishes and the next stroke in the opposite direction has started to form, so it appears a few days after the price turn. Ones that appear earlier are 'pending'; the radar only shows their count and does not draw them.

**Color and size**

Red is buy-type and green is sell-type; a deeper shade means a clearer structure; a bigger bubble means a later type (type 3 is largest). **Shade is not the size of expected returns.**

**Alignment**

When the daily direction agrees with a recent buy/sell point on the 30-minute chart, it is called aligned, meaning two time frames point the same way. It also does **not** guarantee what follows.

**Want the theory**

Read the 9 entries in order under 'Chan primer'; each comes with a diagram.

title: How the four layers relate
summary: Why market, industry and fundamentals are the background, the Chan structure is the price right now, and how to read agreement and disagreement
body:
**Each layer answers a different question**

• **Market**: is overall money flowing with you or against you?
• **Industry**: which industries is money flowing into?
• **Fundamentals**: is the company itself any good?
• **Structure (Chan)**: where on its path is the price right now?

**Slow variables and a fast variable**

Market, industry and fundamentals change slowly, over weeks and months, and describe the **background and causes**: is the environment loose or tight, is the industry in favor, how good is the company. The Chan structure changes fast, over days, and describes **the shape the price has already drawn**: did this leg have enough force, has price left its range.

An analogy: the first three are like weather, terrain and the condition of the car; structure is the speed and steering right now. The weather cannot tell you your speed, and your speed cannot tell you whether a storm is ahead.

**Why structure is only drawn for stocks with strong fundamentals**

Structure signals do not distinguish good companies from bad: a weak company can also show a 'type-1 buy'. The radar first narrows the scope by fundamentals (top 25% by composite grade in the pool), then looks at structure inside it, to focus attention on better companies, not because the signals become more accurate.

**Agreement and disagreement**

• **All pointing the same way**: e.g. a risk-on environment, an industry ahead of the market, a high-grade company and a structure signal on the chart. The picture is more complete, but it is still only a more complete picture, not a guarantee.
• **Contradicting each other**: e.g. a buy-type structure while the industry keeps lagging and the market is risk-off. The contradiction is information: the signal runs against the background, so look more carefully and ask yourself why you want to act here.
• **A layer is missing**: e.g. no fundamentals grade (A-share and Hong Kong rating history is short). Do not pretend the missing layer exists.

**They cannot replace each other, and none predicts**

• A good environment cannot fix a bad structure; good structure cannot fix a bad company.
• All four layers describe what **has already happened**; none tells you what happens tomorrow.
• They are not added into one score or 'rating': summing would hide contradictions, and contradictions are exactly what you most need to see.

**How to use it**

Read from big to small: ask about the environment, then the industry, then the company, and only last the price structure. How each layer is calculated can be opened from the 'How it's calculated' link beside its numbers.

title: Put the four steps together
summary: Walk through one example, then give yourself a checklist
body:
**An example (fictional)**

Say you see a stock called A with a 'type-3 buy' on the radar. How do you use the four steps to understand it?

• **Market**: today is 'risk-on 90%', so money has recently favored offensive sectors and conditions are not a headwind for risk assets. But sentiment says 'fear', so people have not fully relaxed.
• **Industry**: A's industry has +2% relative strength over 20 days, slightly beating the market.
• **Fundamentals**: A's composite grade is A, ahead in its industry, but valuation is on the expensive side.
• **Structure**: A's 'type-3 buy' is established, meaning the first pullback after leaving the pivot did not return into it, so the structure is intact; strength is 'medium'.

Together you get a **picture**: friendly conditions, a slightly strong industry, a company that ranks well but is not cheap, and an intact price structure. What to do next depends on your own judgment and capacity.

**A checklist for yourself**

• Do I understand what each of the four steps says?
• Is there a step I rely on without understanding it? (Tap 'How it's calculated'.)
• What share of my total money is this stock? If it falls 20%, can I accept that?
• Do I want to act because I understand, or because I see others buying?
• Do I know when this view would be proven wrong?

**Finally**

There are no standard answers and the app cannot answer them for you. Their value is that every decision you make has a reason you can see.

title: Common beginner mistakes
summary: A few easy traps and the knowledge behind them
body:
**Treating probability as prediction**

'Risk-on 90%' and 'fundamentals A' describe the **present**; they are not promises about the future. Every probability has its 10% opposite.

**Watching signals but not conditions**

The same 'buy point' means very different things in a headwind market and in a tailwind one. That is why you look at the market and industry first.

**Taking 'good fundamentals' for 'cheap'**

A good company may already have risen a lot. Also look at valuation and where the price is on its structure.

**Chasing gains**

Strong momentum means it rose a lot recently, which also means it is closer to the last pullback. No one can guarantee it continues.

**Not thinking about the worst case**

Every signal and every view can be wrong. How much loss you can bear and what share of your money this is matter far more than which signal is more accurate.

**Treating a tool as the answer**

This app helps you see and understand. It organizes public data and explains the rules, but only you can make the decision.

**A good habit**

Before any decision, try to write the reason in a sentence or two: what I see, why I judge it this way, and when I would admit I was wrong. If you cannot write it, you probably have not thought it through yet.
